summary: The Starling("Astro-Watch", stated in the PDF, is a brand example) is an autonomous, offline wearable health monitoring and emergency rescue software. It is specially designed for astronauts on space missions, varying from multiple space habitats. Because missions to Mars face up to 20-minute one-way communication delays with Earth, astronauts cannot rely on real-time medical support during emergencies. To solve this, the project concludes astronaut smartwatches, biometric chest patches, helmet Heads-Up Displays (HUDs), and WLAN. The smartwatch uses sensor fusion and a real-time "Digital Twin" to combine vital signs (HR, HRV, SpO₂, skin temperature) and daily cognitive memory tests with cabin environmental sensors (CO₂ and radiation), predicting fatigue risks and illnesses before symptoms become critical. When an emergency occurs, an Offline Medical Doctor (OMD) automatically provides guidance (checklists and ultrasound guides) for treatment, filtered by the environment. If a crewmate becomes unresponsive within 10 seconds (likely unconscious), the software triggers an auto-alert, streams live emergency video, and uses Wi-Fi Indoor Positioning System (IPS) triangulation to map their exact location on every crewmate's wrist for rapid rescue.
details:
COMPLETE AND SPECIFIC DETAILS/EXPLANATIONS IN THE FINAL PROJECT PDF!!!

The Starling ("Astro-Watch" stated in the PDF is just a brand example) is an autonomous, offline wearable health monitoring smartwatch, specialised for astronauts on space missions. By the same token, it is a crew rescue system as well, designed for deep-space transit, especially Mars Habitats. Instead of relying on real-time communication with Earth for the sake of medical support, which suffers from delays of 19+ minutes each way, Starling independently replaces that directly inside the aircraft, specifically on the wrists of astronauts.

Every crew member's smartwatches, biometric chest patches, and helmet Heads-Up Displays (HUDs) connect via Bluetooth and a private Habitat WLAN (aka Wireless Local Area Network) to the Mars Habitat Local Server. Henceforth, crew vitals and emergency statuses update live across the team ceaselessly with zero lag, whilst compressed medical logs sync asynchronously to NASA Flight Surgeons on Earth.

The software continuously gathers and fuses physiological biometrics (HR (heart rate), ECG, HRV/RMSSD, blood oxygen (SpO2), skin temperature) with cabin environmental sensors (O2, CO2 ppm, absorbed radiation in mGy) to ensure substantial health and health prediction. It cross-checks physical activity and the current physical state of the user (resting, moving, exercising, space walking...) to eliminate false alarms (example: high HR). An interactive "Digital Twin" is being included to highlight affected organs in red, forecast daily stamina, and predict fatigue risks or illness before symptoms escalate and become critical.

Tracking of cognitive and sleep readiness is part of this software. Memory tests with 5 random questions of pattern/symbol matching that measure thinking accuracy, reaction latency, and sleep stages (REM, N1-N3) to schedule high-stakes EVAs during an astronaut's peak cognitive window.

Furthermore, astronauts ought to select their active mission environment (ISS, Transit Spacecraft, Lunar Base, or Mars Habitat) so that the OMD (Offline Medical Doctor) AI filters out irrelevant rules and loads specialised offline treatment checklists. During an emergency, OMD automatically launches step-by-step interactive checklists (such as Martian perchlorate dust inhalation or solar storm shelter protocols) and handheld ultrasound probe guides, plus an everyday offline medical library for crew training if needed.

If an astronaut presses the physical button (emergency button located on the chest/beside the watch), shouts "HELP", or fails to respond to an anomaly alert within 10 seconds (either to cancel it because of a false alert or to deal the anomaly to him/herself), the Starling senses it as an "unconscious astronaut" and then triggers flashing lights, a loud alarm, live emergency camera streaming on the watch, and a Wi-Fi Indoor Positioning System (IPS). Using RSSI triangulation from at least three habitat access point pins, the exact room and distance of every member are on a live 2D map.

The benefits and impact of Starling:

- Enables instant offline diagnosis and treatment through OMD without waiting 20-40 minutes for Earth replies

- Faster unconscious crew being rescued with the contribution of Wi-Fi IPS triangulation guidance

- Prevents astronauts from overworking and EVA accidents by alerting crew planners when there is radiation, poor-quality air in the cabin, or sleep loss that degrades an astronaut's physical stamina or memory.

- Easy and quick health monitoring, specifically the vitals.

- Built-in ECG

- Multi-functional

- Includes "Members' Status", which is able to display every member's HR, SpO₂, skin temperature and IPS. Pressing into a member who is in emergency will additionally display the cause of the anomaly, how the problem occurred, what the problem is and the solution (treatment).

The creativity we casted:

- Most medical apps treat all environments identically. Our idea of Environment Mode Switching and Selector prevents false alerts (for example, distinguishing lunar rover vibrations from a Martian dust storm) and speeds up OMD AI's processing during real emergencies.

- During spacewalks, astronauts usually have a hard time trying to visualise screens from the watches; thus, we designed a synchronised Helmet HUD that displays main biometric data: vitals, radiation exposure in mGy, personal digital twin. Not only those, during spacewalking, perchance a crewmate/yourself could be in trouble of emergency; hence, installing notification of alerts visually can be effective. To ensure the astronaut who is spacewalking doesn't get stressed out quickly, distracting audio from the alert system is turned off inside the helmet HUD. If it's a false alert, the astronaut can say "Cancel" to cancel the visual alert in the helmet HUD.

- A dull and ubiquitous navigation bar is being replaced by a 360-degree twist-and-select navigation wheel. The navigation wheel allows users to have an easy way to open other pages or screens rather than pressing exits and crosses at the corner of the watch.

- Instead of pressing an interactive button in the smartwatch to open the navigation wheel, we made it easier. Press and hold the button at the side of the watch to open the navigation wheel, twist/roll the button to decide/choose, and let go to select. Subsequently, this way of opening the navigation wheel also opens the complete 2D map with every crewmate and where they are. Tap on the map to full screen the map.

- Live camera feeds remaining off during normal operations facilitates battery conservation. On the contrary, live camera streams automatically only when an anomaly is detected or an emergency/notification of alert.

- After the user is awake for 10 minutes, let the user do check-ins on the user's health using yes/no questions to check for any symptoms and objective questions to challenge the user's intellectual thinking with math questions and general knowledge about the things on Earth (which can also keep the user on track with Earth's nature); if the user isn't awake yet, vibrate and ring like an alarm to wake up the user after ample sleeping.

- Spoken step-by-step medical guides allow injured astronauts to follow medical instructions hand-free. This also resolves the problem of tiredness from squinting ones' eyes just to visualise the guide.

- Instead of just an offline medical doctor AI, we added a feature where astronauts can search for already-prepared medical guides packed in PDF files to learn beforehand just in case of an emergency where OMN AI unfortunately isn't available

- Due to the lack of coding experiences and skills, my teammate and I decided to make things different by using hand-drawn technical blueprints as our project completion for this challenge.

Factors my team considered:

- Cybersecurity and anti-hack protection inspired by the German Aerospace Center (DLR) SOLISS local-storage study: all biometric and location data is encrypted at rest locally on the smartwatches and air-gapped Habitat WLAN, avoiding weak and vulnerable external cloud servers and preventing biometric spoofing.

- Audio speakers in the members' status remain muted until an actual emergency occurs to prevent alarm fatigue

- Voice-to-text mechanisms can prevent members' frustration from texting on small screens alongside quickening the process of searching files/asking AI/replying AI.

- Other common health problems faced by astronauts in space and their treatment or measures. Bone/muscle loss (ARED resistance workouts, 2 hours of daily workouts, 6 days a week), radiation (water-lined radiation trackers, retreating to heavily shielded modules), everyday symptoms, like nausea, sleep, and congestion (anti-nausea pills, decongestants, and sleeping aids), and emergencies & diagnostics (portable ultrasounds, eye scanners, and detribillators)


What we used to create this project:

- Tools: Fong Zhen Herng used a Huawei MatePad+Stylus for digital drawing, UI wireframing, and taking notes; Adeliz used real stationery and papers to draft, take notes, and draw.

- Link: Google Drive
- Coding Languages: None

- Hardware: tablet, stylus, laptop

- Software: Google Drive, Notes, PDFs, Gemini AI for deep researching and understanding of the given requirement
